# 18-careforce — sources

Back-test entry `18-careforce.yaml`: Careforce, AI agents that call and book the patients a health center never reaches
(YC Fall 2024). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named.
"Author's choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the
Launch YC post of 2024-11-22 and the weeks around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later, and a later price sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Careforce - Must-have AI agents for Healthcare admin", 2024-11-22 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/MJj-careforce-must-have-ai-agents-for-healthcare-admin
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/careforce
- [WB] careforce.ai in the Wayback Machine: snapshots of 2024-05-09 and 2024-05-18 (a near-empty page, no pricing), then none until 2025-11-13 — https://web.archive.org/web/20240518050058/https://careforce.ai/ ; index https://web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=careforce.ai
- [KFF] KFF Health News, Kern Family Health Care's Medi-Cal renewals with Careforce, 2026-08-04 — https://kffhealthnews.org/medicaid/medicaid-work-requirements-medi-cal-ai-agents-reenroll-careforce-california/
- [CHCF] California Health Care Foundation investment page (CHCF is an investor, $500,000, February 2026; the page blocks direct fetches, so the quote is as the diversity research recorded it) — https://www.chcf.org/investment/careforce/
- [SITE] careforce.ai, read 2026-10-22 (no pricing; /pricing returns 404) — https://careforce.ai/
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, medical assistants, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/medical-assistants.htm

No Launch HN exists (HN search for Careforce, read 2026-10-22: https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/search?query=Careforce&tags=story).

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Medical assistants at community health centers, who work the outreach lists between patients.
   [LYC] "For health centers & practices this means MAs (short-staffed with front desk and intake) end up spending most
   of their time on admin tasks and most patients are never outreached & scheduled for vital screenings/visits,
   leaving a 1/3rd of care unserviced." → `roles[assistant]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: of
   [LYC]'s three segments (health centers and practices; digital health and CCM companies; payers) the first, the one
   the post describes by its staff.

2. **What (the job).** Get every patient due for a screening or visit called and booked.
   [LYC] "Most care coordination & data sharing is still manually done by staff through phones, email, fax because of
   unintegrated systems and custom workflows too unique to automate out of the box." → `statements.problem`,
   `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** Each working day, when the list of due patients has to be called between patients.
   [LYC] "Outreach using 50+ editable scripts (mammograms, pre-post-op, onboarding etc.)"; "Leave Voicemails, Sending
   reminders, and autonomously retry patients as needed". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: outreach call list`.
   Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (spec 120: a daily rhythm in a clinic read as working days) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; [LYC] gives no count. Prevalence `p_80_100` follows from "most patients are
   never outreached".

4. **Which people.** US community health centers (FQHCs) and primary-care practices that work outreach lists by phone.
   [LYC] "Our AI agents are already Live with health centers and digital health companies helping analyze, call,
   schedule, and generate revenue." → `context.segment`, `market: US` (a San Francisco company, [KFF]).

5. **Who pays.** The health center. [LYC] "Let us take on your calling, coordination, and manual admin work so you can
   get more patients in the door without burning out your staff."; "increase revenue with Careforce AI Agents".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: director}`. Author's choice: the decider is the health center's executive or
   operations director and the tested role "The CFO" (a second role, "The board", listed: FQHCs are governed by
   boards). Purchase friction's three items (a HIPAA security review — tested; giving the agent access to the EMR; a
   board vote) are the author's, from [LYC]'s "Use EMR, Scheduling, payer and provider portals through UI or API
   Integrations" and [KFF]'s note that plans "are responsible for ensuring that technology complies with state and
   federal regulations, including patient privacy and data security". Commitment's step, "try it on one outreach list":
   [LYC] "We'd love to learn about your use cases and give you personalized demos unique to your use case."; the
   wording is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** Two agents: one calls, texts, emails and books; one pulls data and builds the lists.
   [LYC] "Careforce creates autonomous agents that are able to take on these human-glue tasks and complete them in the
   same way as your staff would without the need for integrations." [LYC] (Angelica) "Call, text, email, and schedule
   patients autonomously"; "Speak in 29 Languages to engage and educate across demographics"; "Make 100 calls / min.
   and finish a year's worth of outreach in weeks". [LYC] (David) "Prepare reports, and generate lists for Angelica to
   realize the unrealized revenue". → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`; Compatibility (the list straight out
   of the EMR — tested; open slots; patients picking up unknown numbers) and Adoption friction (hand the day's list to
   an AI caller — tested; take the calls it hands back, from [KFF] "This will always be, in my opinion, an AI-human
   combination"). Relative advantage's two benefits are [LYC]'s retries (fewer_attempts) and "finish a year's worth
   of outreach in weeks" (shorter_time); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price is public at launch or today: [LYC] offers demos, [WB] has no pricing page near launch,
   [SITE] has none today. The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$1,500 to $3,000 per health center a month**, is the
   operator's reading: a monthly per-site fee of the size community health centers pay for a part-time outreach caller's
   share of work (an MA's hour is about $22, [BLS]; $1,500 to $3,000 is roughly 70 to 135 such hours), set below what
   the bookings it claims to recover would bring in. It is said in `statements.commercial` as the founder would type
   it, and marked there and in the header as the operator's.
   Existing sacrifice, RATE about **30% to 33%** of the patients due for a visit or screening per health center a month,
   lost as "Visits and screenings never booked because nobody reached the patient": [LYC]'s "1/3rd of care unserviced"
   for health centers (33%) and "costing 30% in bookings" across healthcare (30%). Ability to pay is read `budget` by
   the engine (a percent of patients never compares with an amount a month), so the directors answer the budget item.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from [LYC]'s scripts list (mammograms, pre-post-op), the short-staffing it
   names, and [KFF]; no respondent is a real person. [KFF] (Kern's CEO) "But we are already stretched thin. We need this
   functionality to be much more effective and augment our efforts." [KFF] "In samples of actual conversations provided
   to a reporter, Angelica sounded lifelike at first, although more than once cross-talk with a patient caused the
   program to pause suddenly."

- Thanh Nguyen → [LYC] "Speak in 29 Languages"; [KFF] a member who valued being called in Spanish; an MA who calls the Vietnamese-speaking patients herself is the author's.

- Olga Petrenko → author's invention, filling a gap: a practice with a dedicated outreach coordinator whose list gets done, so the problem is not a chorus (against on Importance).
- Marisol Vega → author's invention: a chipped (rather_not_say) story, GUESSED by code.
- Darnell Hayes → author's invention: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED).
- Fatima Al-Sayed, Brandon Kealoha → author's invention: gate No (no outreach list worked in the window).
- Rosa Jimenez → [KFF] "it took her a minute before she realized she wasn't speaking with a human" and the cross-talk pauses, turned sceptical: older patients who hang up on a recording (Relative advantage negative).
- Abena Owusu → [LYC] "unintegrated systems" and [LYC] (David) "Use UI to download data across EMRs & portals"; a list built by hand fails the tested condition (Compatibility no).
- Priyanka Shah → author's invention, filling a gap: bookings into blocked slots, so she would not hand the list over (Adoption friction probably not).
- Miguel Ferreira → [LYC] "care coordination" staff; a care coordinator works the list (the Current-solution escape, someone_else_checks).

Health center directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Linda Okafor-Reyes, Harold Jensen → [LYC] "increase revenue" and "book 30% more appointments": directors who pay at the founder's band.
- Samuel Goldberg → author's invention: would pay above the band but tests first.
- Carmen Ruiz → author's invention: pays below the band until bookings are shown.
- Aisha Bello → author's invention, filling a gap: a health center booked out for weeks, so unbooked patients cost it nothing it counts (Nothing; would not pay).
- Richard Lam → [KFF] the privacy and data-security duty; a director who cannot say the cost or the price (both escapes).
- Nadia Haddad → [KFF] "an AI-human combination"; a pilot with staff listening in.

The split on Price (4 of the 7 who name a rung at $1,500 or above) is the author's: no public account gives what a
health center would pay. No respondent carries the name of a customer, patient, official or founder in the sources.

## Status today

Same idea, traction moved to health plans. [SITE] still sells the two agents for payors, plans, FQHCs and specialties.
The public customers are Medi-Cal health plans doing renewal outreach: [KFF] "Kern Family has spent about $370,000 on the
software by Careforce, a San Francisco startup, to facilitate rapid and repeated outreach to members when it's time to
renew their coverage."; "estimated it would have had to spend $2.4 million in staffing costs to match the program's more
than 800,000 calls to its 387,000 members"; "Kern Family's Medi-Cal renewal rate in April was 94.9%". [CHCF] "With the
aid of Careforce, KFHC renewed 96% of their members during the first year, compared to 38% before using the AI platform."
[KFF] says the agent "speaks more than 30 languages" (29 at launch). Price today: not public.

## Could not be sourced

- **A price, at any time.** The founder's $1,500 to $3,000 per health center a month is the operator's reading (item 7);
  the only public money figure is one health plan's cumulative spend ([KFF], 2026), not a unit price.
- **A health center's share of patients never booked, measured.** The 30% to 33% are the founders' own launch claims
  (one for health centers, one for healthcare overall), not a study.
- **A buyer title.** [LYC] asks "Healthcare Orgs" for demos; the director as decider, the CFO and the board as the roles,
  and the three Purchase friction items are the author's.
- **First-person MA accounts.** None public; the occasions are scripted from [LYC] and [KFF] (a health plan, not a
  health center).
- **A launch-era site.** [WB] holds no snapshot between 2024-05-18 and 2025-11-13; the launch post is the only
  launch-era page. [CHCF] could not be fetched directly (a bot check); its quote is as the diversity research read it.
- An MA's hour: [BLS]'s median stands in; no cost in the entry is in hours.

founder.order_why: The recency question (screen 4) sits between the two halves of the context, so screen 5 reopens the context framing after I had already moved on to timing, when the window would read more naturally after the context was fully defined.

screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (I send each one their own link) / People from a Keel contact list (Keel makes a link for each; I send them) / A group, with one open link (I post it where they already are; each signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' is stated with '4 answered' beside it, but the 5 needed sits only on the cards, and the line names only Frequency when Importance and Current solution are short too.
screens.why_b2: The tally '1 holding · 3 too few · 7 people answered' is plain, but I need a second look to see why only 4 of the 7 count on three cards when 6 said yes on Prevalence.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are my lines word for word, but Prevalence and Frequency say medical assistants 'got every patient ... called and booked', which is the opposite of my problem, since most due patients are never reached.
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: whether to send the study to more medical assistants, how many more, or what the one holding card means for Careforce.
screens.why_b5: The 'too few' cards are honest about n, but 'Holding up' at 6 of 7, sitting exactly at the bar, reads as if the job gets done, with no note that seven is a small count or that the wording flips my claim.
screens.instead: Not called yet: only 4 of the 7 medical assistants answered Frequency, Importance and Current solution, and each needs 5, so send the study to a few more MAs who worked an outreach list this week; 6 of 7 did work one, which is just at the bar.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 for and 1 against on a 0 to 7 axis with the marker at 6, but I have to look twice to see that a "yes" means 'I had a due list to work this week' and not 'I got everyone booked'.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence and the clinic's outreach list are mine, but the line "got every patient who is due ... called and booked" reads as if my MAs finished the list, which is the opposite of my pain: most due patients are never reached.
screens.why_b4: "How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards" only sends me onward; it does not say what a common list means for selling to health centers.
screens.why_b5: n=7 and "a lean, not a call" are on the screen, but six people who "said yes" to "did you get every patient called and booked" can read as six MAs who have no problem, and that softly misleads.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 medical assistants had a list of due patients to call in the last 5 working days (only Fatima had none), right at your bar of 8 in 10, with 7 people a lean; next, see how often it comes round and whether it ranks in their top two.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside "5 needed to call it" and the So line ties them with "4 counted, 5 needed", though the verdict's "4 answered" clashes with the count line's "6 answered" and should say "4 counted".
screens.why_b2: The axis of working days out of 5 and the median at 4 read at once, but "your bar · 3 of 4" next to "5 needed" and a strip with a ghost cell took me a second look to work out how many people and where the bar actually sits.
screens.why_b3: It is my job phrase stitched onto my 3-to-5-days frequency, but "get every patient called and booked on 3 to 5 days" reads like the job being done, the opposite of my pitch that a third of care goes unserviced, and the truncated question ("get every patient who is due?") with "the most recent time it happened" on a count of days isn't how I'd ask it.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is honest but generic; it doesn't tell me that one more counted MA would settle it, or that all four counted so far sit inside my range.
screens.why_b5: No overreach: the low n is named twice ("too few to call", "a small group: a lean, not a call"), the two uncounted answers are named with their reasons, and nothing is called holding.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 6 MAs answered, 4 counted, and all 4 work the due list on 3 to 5 days (middle answer 4). One more counted answer settles it, so send the study to one or two more MAs.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 counted, 5 needed', but its line says '4 answered' while the count line says '6 answered · 4 counted', so I have to work out which is true.
screens.why_b2: The bars count 8 picks but the bar is 3 of 4 people, and the strip shows 'for 3, against 5' as if 8 people answered, so I need a second look to see that 3 of my 4 counted MAs picked it.
screens.why_b3: The title is Importance and the belief line is the one I checked, word for word: getting due patients called and booked is one of the two hardest things.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it doesn't say that 3 of 4 already meets my bar, that one more counted answer would decide it, or that Olga's coordinator is the case against.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', but '4 answered' (it was 6) and the five 'against' cells, which are picks rather than people, soften the record.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 6 answered, 4 counted (Marisol declined, Darnell guessed), 5 needed. 3 of 4 put calling and booking in their two, which meets your 2-in-3 bar, so get one or two more clean answers. The one against (Olga) has a coordinator who clears the list daily.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 answered · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats it as 4 counted, 5 needed.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts last-list outcomes over 4 people. But 'your bar · 3 of 4' reads like both the bar and the tally, and the strip's one ghost cell (six answered, two not counted) took me a second look to understand as the fifth answer still missing.
screens.why_b3: The title 'Current solution' and the belief line are word for word what I checked, and the bar line restates my 2-in-3 below 'Most called; a few left for tomorrow'.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me that one more counted medical assistant would decide it, or that the 3 of 4 already leaning my way is worth chasing.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible throughout, the two uncounted answers are named with reasons, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps the 3 of 4 from being sold as a held belief.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 counted, 5 needed. 3 of 4 say today's calling fell short, which leans your way. One more medical assistant's answer on their last outreach list would settle it.

screens.why1: Asking about my outreach list first makes sense, but it asks whether I finished the job instead of whether I had a list to call, so a 'No' (the honest answer most days at my center) would end the study for exactly the people who struggle with it.
screens.why2: 'Called and booked' is two things in one: I can call everyone on the list and still book only half because nobody picks up, so I don't know whether to say yes or no.
screens.why3: Working the due-list between rooming patients is my daily work, so I know exactly how the last five days went.
screens.why4: Yes or No can't hold 'called them all but couldn't book them all', a gate should have no escape, yet there are two, and 'I'd rather not say' plus 'I can't recall one particular outreach list' are awkward and redundant.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product leaks, but the founder's goal is pasted in as the gate question, so it measures success instead of whether I face the list at all.
screens.why6: It is short and ends 'Yes or no', but hearing 'called and booked' in one breath makes me stop and work out which half I'm answering.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you have a list of patients due for a screening or visit to call? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I got my whole due list called and booked, asking on how many of those five days I managed it follows naturally.
screens.why2: The question stops at "get every patient who is due" and never says called and booked or due for what, so I wouldn't know if it means roomed, seen, or called off the outreach list.
screens.why3: I work the call list every day between rooming, so I know which days I got through it and which days it rolled over.
screens.why4: There's no zero, and with us short at the front desk and intake, the honest answer for a lot of us is that I didn't finish the list on any of those days.
screens.why5: Cutting off "for a screening or visit called and booked" loses the actual job, so it no longer asks about the calling and booking at all.
screens.why6: It's short and "a number from 1 to 5" says well, but heard aloud the stem sounds unfinished and I'd wait for the rest of the sentence.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, on how many days did you get every patient due for a screening or visit called and booked? None; 1; 2; 3; 4; or all 5. Or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: After asking whether I got everyone called and on how many days, it makes sense to ask which part of my week I'd most want lightened, with the call list as one choice among my real jobs.
screens.why2: Phones and refill requests, prior auths, rooming and vitals, and covering check-in are exactly how we talk about the work, so I can answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: These are the things I juggle every clinic day, especially getting pulled to the front desk when we're short, so I know my answer without guessing.
screens.why4: The five are distinct, cover my day well, and are in my words, and 'None of these' fits; charting is the only big one left out.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's job of getting due patients called and booked as one plain option, with no product or company terms reaching me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with five short, parallel options I can hold, and a single escape said last; 'rooming patients and taking vitals on time' is the longest but still says fine.

screens.why1: It fits after asking what I'd want easier, but screens 1 and 2 already asked whether I got every patient called and booked, so the top option repeats something I've answered.
screens.why2: 'Calling, texting patients' reads like a word is missing and asks about two things at once, and 'due for a visit' leaves out the screenings that are most of my list.
screens.why3: Working the outreach list between rooming patients is exactly what I do every day, so I can answer from my last list.
screens.why4: 'Most called', 'part of it' and 'a handful' blur together, 'between patients' says when rather than how much, and the options mix called with booked; 'Someone else did it' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: It's meant to ask how well the way I work the list is going for me, but it drifted into asking how far down the list I got.
screens.why6: 'Calling, texting patients' stumbles when said, and each option is two clauses held together by a pause, which is a lot to hold across five.
screens.instead: Think of your last outreach list. How well did working it by phone go for you? I'll read four options: it went fine; it went okay but took too long; it was hard to fit between patients; or it mostly didn't get done. Or say someone else did it.
